units.label: Matching Pennies人类与模型输出随机性
units.description: 100轮序列与逐轮n-gram猜测者对战；单独比较胜率和游程检验。

facts.statement: 研究给定数值语境所隐含的客观概率P与模型后继token概率Π是否匹配；这不同于回答正确率对应的置信度校准。

method_function.text: 把校准对象限定为语境概率分布，避免混同正确性置信度。

facts.statement: 颜色任务交叉5模板、3数值尺度各100组合与110有序颜色对（55无序对），共165K题；尺度为1–10、从10–100取10数及从100–999取10数。

method_function.text: 交叉数量、词项身份和顺序以识别数量敏感性与选项偏差。

facts.statement: 文字应用题使用10模板、相同3尺度各100数值组合，每模板4–10选项对；Table1报告33.6K题。

method_function.text: 检验比例判断是否跨具体语境成立；不据总量自行补全缺失模板。

facts.statement: 均匀区间任务以区间内整数为有效候选，改变端点包含方式；正文称5模板、320端点对、范围10–1000、区间长度小于10并作单token预测；Table1报告4.5K题，附录实际列4模板。

method_function.text: 用明确均匀分布为目标分布，并保留模板数量冲突。

facts.statement: 实验比较8组开源Base/Chat配对及4个GPT模型；Chat同时指既有指令微调版本和显式校准提示。作者未报告自行训练这些LLM。

method_function.text: 记录模型与提示共同构成的比较条件，不将差异归为纯训练因果效应。

facts.statement: 聊天提示包含用户要求按语境概率生成一个词/token、预置assistant确认以及用户题目；颜色/应用题给5种提示，分布任务另给提示。

method_function.text: 明确角色、输出约束和预填回复；不误写为生成的思维链。

facts.statement: 读取候选词的模型概率，并将常见大小写与空格token变体相加；候选集合T只是全词表子集，并不涵盖所有语法上可能的续写。

method_function.text: 区分词项概率合并与候选外概率损失。

facts.statement: PM为候选T上的概率和；正文以0.30低质量、>0.75较充分作说明，并非在此定义统一过滤阈值。WD使用SciPy wasserstein_distance_nd；RE定义为H(Π)−H(P)，负值表示过度集中、正值表示过度分散。

method_function.text: 并列区分有效输出质量、分布距离和熵差，不把RE写为KL。

facts.statement: 作者因目标概率可能为零而未采用KL；并称曾算MSE、结论无实质区别，故仅报告WD。

method_function.text: 记录指标选择理由和有限的替代指标检查。

facts.statement: 参考行为为Null、理想校准、总选较高/较低概率、总选第一/第二选项；额外Pick Higher(q)将q放在较高概率选项、其余均分，随机基线抽两个U(0,1)数后以温度softmax。

method_function.text: 用可解释行为基准刻画错误类型，非拟合探针分类器。

facts.statement: 作者按选项对聚类计算标准误并显示95%置信区间；表格±为CI，Table1熵的下标另表示题目间方差。

method_function.text: 分清依赖结构与不同误差标记，避免把所有下标都解释为SE。

facts.statement: 在颜色及应用题中，作者报告Pick Higher(q=.7)的WD优于所测模型；因此任务表现并非仅凭常规正确率衡量。

method_function.text: 用分布敏感指标与简易概率基准给主发现定标。

facts.statement: 作者将Chat相对Base的低熵倾向解释为指令微调后的mode collapse；本提取保留其解释性质，因比较同时改变提示与既有模型版本。

method_function.text: 分开观察到的分布集中与未经随机控制的机制解释。

facts.statement: 相容性热图按数值组合网格统计行为相容比例，颜色标最大比例对应的行为；不同于按WD最近参考点分类的热图。

method_function.text: 避免把两种图的颜色和数值当同一指标。

facts.statement: 最近参考行为分类以数值尺度×模板×选项对的一组结果为单位，计算与参考行为WD；网格平均PM<.5时标Null。

method_function.text: 把阈值用于作者指定的分组分类层，不擅自扩作所有数据筛除。

facts.statement: 比较同一颜色先/后出现时的校准与排序，并以Spearman和Kendall相关比较模型间层级；Table14仅显示所选择的显著相关。白色先出现改善校准不等于模型偏爱选白色。

method_function.text: 用身份与顺序交叉识别偏差，同时限定排序含义。

facts.statement: 以gpt-4o-2024-08-06生成500条1–10句引导前缀及500个新颜色模板，在部分指令模型上检验结论对材料扩展的稳定性；作者承认合成材料风险。

method_function.text: 提示和材料扰动是稳健性检查，不是训练或新增独立人群实验。

facts.statement: 用8、9、48、51、98、99的小集合展示成功与失败实例；额外图以WD<.05记解决，报告以.01阈值趋势相近。

method_function.text: 说明偶尔成功与总体失准可同时成立，并记录阈值敏感性。

facts.statement: Mode Probability为全题平均maxΠ，Mode Stability为Base/Chat最大概率token相同的比例。

method_function.text: 分别量化集中程度与既有模式保留，避免混成准确率。

facts.statement: Mode Frequency把区间按底层数字范围与包含方式分组，例如[2,5)与[132,135)；先温度0取贪心输出，再组内保留数字维度平均、取各组最大频率、最后跨组平均。

method_function.text: 检测跨等价区间的数字偏向，区别于单题概率最大值。

facts.statement: 由于真实训练语料未知，以infini-gram查询3万亿token Dolma作为数字频率代理；查询在数字前后加空格以减少数字子串混入。

method_function.text: 记录外部语料代理和边界匹配规则，不将代理当成训练日志。

facts.statement: 以Spearman检验WD与Frequency Gap=log|Freq(N1)−Freq(N2)|的相关；Table6突出p<.01。更广数字范围与混合效应模型是未来建议。

method_function.text: 把已实施相关分析与未实施的混合效应控制分开。

facts.statement: 附录用Matching Pennies比较人类和模型是否能输出难以预测的序列；猜测者匹配出币得+1否则−1，理想策略为随机化。作者承认随机输出不能唯一证明内部概率已校准。

method_function.text: 将输出层随机性与内部概率校准分开。

facts.statement: 每局100轮，模型扮misleader，guesser对第i轮仅用先前m_j(j<i)；模型采样温度1，10名技术背景志愿者提供44局、每人最多10局。

method_function.text: 保留序列时间方向以及游戏嵌套于人的结构。

facts.statement: 模型和人均被明确要求随机；作者报告不作此要求模型表现接近0。正式报告4-gram猜测者，称1–5 gram表现相近。

method_function.text: 记录指令操纵和对手阶数稳健性，不补造未报告条件样本数。

facts.statement: Fig24对手从已见序列统计n+1转移频数，依据最后n项选更常见后继；空序列选H、只有一项时翻转、历史过短递减n、转移平局或未见模式选H。这是随历史更新的经验预测器，不涉及LLM权重训练。

method_function.text: 明确自适应对手实现；不能仅称固定随机对手或完全无学习组件。

facts.statement: PWR为misleader胜率，模型按100局、每局最多100轮平均；人类为已述44局。WW为100项序列在α=.05的Wald–Wolfowitz游程检验中未被判非随机的比例。

method_function.text: 分清模型与人类样本量，失败于拒绝随机性不等于证明随机。

facts.statement: Table8随机Python序列PWR=.50/WW=.98，人类.33/.07；GPT3.5为.40/.43、GPT4Turbo为.33/.25、GPT4o为.36/.19。

method_function.text: 提供两种随机性相关操作指标，保留其不等价性。

facts.statement: Table9列出完整模型键，其中GPT快照为3.5-turbo-0125、4-turbo-2024-04-09、4o-2024-08-06、4o-mini-2024-07-18；作者称数据和实验将经Drive发布，8张A100约48小时可运行。该时间为论文报告，未在此复跑。

method_function.text: 保存版本和计算声明的来源，区分作者承诺与已验证资源。

facts.statement: 参考行为只描述跨大量平衡实例的行为相容性，同一单题可兼容多个解释；不构成对内部认知机制的直接识别。

method_function.text: 防止从热图标签直接推断模型内部策略。

What Do We Mean By Calibration?
LMs’ output probabilities are calibrated to
their contexts if the probabilities of relevant
tokens correspond to the numeric content
implicitly or explicitly defined in those contexts. If tokens t1 , t2 , . . . , tn are indicated
by context C to have probabilities P =
p1 , p2 , . . . , pn , a calibrated LM m outputs
corresponding probabilities πi = m(ti |C):

Introduction

pi ∝ πi ,

We investigate if language model (LM) outputs are
calibrated to the numeric content of their contexts.
Consider the context below:

i ∈ 1, 2, . . . , n.

We set calibration as the distance between
P and Π = π1 , π2 , . . . , πn (Section 3.2).

(1) From 98 blue marbles and 99 red marbles, Tommy reached blindly into a bag
and grabbed a marble the color [blue/red]

Models struggle to calibrate internal uncertainty with textual outputs. A related line of
work studies how well models calibrate prediction
confidence with prediction accuracy: a calibrated
model with 0.80 confidence on each prediction
should classify 80% of examples correctly (Guo
et al., 2017; Minderer et al., 2021). Under this
definition, Wei et al. (2024) reports GPT models
have good calibration, whereas, Phan et al. (2025)
reports the opposite. Another line of work investigates how well model outputs align with uncertainty (Yona et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2024; Zhou
et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2022), termed linguistic calibration (Mielke et al., 2022). Yona et al. (2024)
reports that models struggle to exhibit internal uncertainty in text. Kumar et al. (2024) measures
how well confidence is aligned internally (model
probabilities) and externally (via eliciting a model
to choose among a Likert scale). In our work, we
look at the agreement between the probability of
predicted outputs and the contextually defined likelihood of outputs in the text. We find that models
are often internally certain when they should be
uncertain; this mode collapse arises both via supervised fine-tuning and reward-based fine-tuning
(O’Mahony et al., 2024; Janus, 2022). Zhou et al.

We introduce three templated datasets. Each
problem instance is a context C to be continued by a relevant token among t1 , t2 , . . . , tn =
T ⊂ V , where V is the full vocabulary. Each
token ti is associated with an implied probability pi , forming a distribution over T , P =
p1 , p2 , . . . , pn . In Example 1, T is {red, blue}
with P = {red : 98/197, blue : 99/197}. For a
model m, we define Π = π1 , π2 , . . . , πn where
πi ≈ m(ti |C), with one modification. We sum
the probabilities of common tokenizations for a
given word,
namely, capitalization and spaces:
P
πi =
s∈Tokenizations(ti ) m(s|C). For example,
for the option red, we sum probabilities for “red”,
“Red”, “_red”, and “_Red.” This approach does not
account for the problem of there being many ways
of grammatically continuing the sentence. However, empirically, instruction-tuned models put almost all probability mass on T . This admittedly
imperfect approach still allows us to study the problem meaningfully.1

We use three metrics to test if models calibrate to
numeric contexts and where they go wrong.
Probability Mass (PM): A model’s calibration,
the relative probability mass across tokens in T, is
well-founded only if there is sufficient probability mass upon the tokens in TP
. We measure this
.
directly with PM, PM(T ) = t ∈ T πt . If PM(T )
for a model is low (say, 0.30), then it is unclear
if the model is capturing the intended relationship
between the context and T . While meaningful distribution across T could still exist if these values
were normalized, we set this case aside. When
PM is high (say, > 0.75), we can start to meaningfully ask questions about how probability mass is
allocated among, say, red and blue.
Wasserstein Distance (WD): To measure calibration, we use WD (Kantorovich, 1939), which
captures the movement between one distribution
(or set of values) and another.2 We use SciPy’s
wasserstein_distance_nd implementation.3
Relative Entropy (RE): To help understand a
model’s behavior, we propose RE = H(Π)−H(P ),
the difference in entropy H between model and
ideal calibrated probabilities. RE < 0 means the
model’s probabilities are overly concentrated and
RE > 0 means they are overly diffuse.

Our experiments assume access to model logits.
We test range of open-source models with
both base and instruction-tuned versions available:
Mistral-7B-v0.1, Mistral-7B-v0.3,
Mixtral-8x7B-v0.1, Yi-1.5-9B, Yi-1.5-34B,
Llama-3.1-8B, gemma-2-9b,
gemma-2-27b
(Jiang et al., 2023, 2024; Young et al., 2024;
Dubey et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024); and four
proprietary models, gpt-3.5, gpt-4-turbo,
gpt-4o-mini, and gpt-4o (Brown et al., 2020;
Achiam et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2024). We prompt
instruction-tuned models to calibrate outputs to the
numbers in context. We refer to the base version
of the models as “Base” and the instruction-tuned,
prompted models as “Chat.”

For (a) colors, we use 5 templates, 3 numeric
scales with 100 configurations each, and 110 permutations of color options (e.g., red/blue and
blue/red).5 The numeric scales are (1) numbers
1 to 10, (2) ten numbers sampled from 10 to 100,
and (3) ten numbers sampled from 100 to 999. Pilot experiments with larger numbers (> 1000) did
not see marked differences in calibration. Still,
future work should study a wider range of numbers. For (b) wordproblems, there are 10 templates,
the same 3 numeric scales with 100 configurations
each, and 4-10 pairs of options (e.g., spruce/cedar,
or nurse/doctor) depending on the template. For
(c) distributions, the configuration is different. The
task is to pick a number uniformly from an interval.
The valid options in T are all integers in the interval.
There are 5 templates, different range inclusivities,
and 320 pairs of numbers that define the intervals
ranging from 10 to 1000. Each problem is set to
occur within an interval length of less than 10 and
requires only a single token prediction.

of data. We do this by 1) introducing variations

Specifically, using gpt-4o-2024-08-06, we create
500 leading introductions to prefix our templates
in the colors dataset, ranging from one to ten sentences. Next, we create 500 more templates for
the colors dataset using gpt-4o-2024-08-06. For
both new splits we test a subset of our instructiontuned models. The calibration scores did changed
little from the original performances, Table 7. In
two cases, the calibration was worse (the confidence interval was strictly positive), though the
effect was not large. Using synthetically generated data has its risks, nonetheless, we take these
results as evidence that calibration over a wider
distribution of similar data remains poor.

shown as such for visual acuity. For these plots we
considered the model to have solved an instance if

fit. Making this threshold more strict, say, 0.01,
maintains the trends present in the figure. Mostly,
these plots show that (1) in some cases the models

differ per model but again mirror previous results.
The most important result is the first. Models are
clearly capable of yielding calibrated probabilties, but do not do so in the (large) majority of

Our experiments demonstrated that language models are poorly calibrated. Here, we provide further
context by comparing the proprietary model and
human behavior, asking if models are as random
(or not) as people. Previous work suggests that
both would be not random (see our Related Work
section). We test this again. To get at this question,
we use a variation of the two-player game Matching Pennies. We focus on a variation of the game
similar to Eliaz and Rubinstein (2011). Each round,
the “guesser” aims to match her chosen coin face
with “misleader’s” choice, earning a +1 reward if
their coin faces match, and -1 otherwise. The Nash
Equilibrium is for both agents to act randomly. A
calibrated model can trivially achieve random behavior.

This experiment is based on a simple heads/tails
game. Our motivation for including this experiment is to allow a human baseline in a setting
where random behavior is optimal. This section
makes no distinction between calibrated probabilities and unbiased outputs because we don’t have
access to this information for humans. However,
to “perform” well, or appear calibrated, requires
either the model/person to (1) produce calibrated
probabilities which when sampled from will yield
random outputs, (2) use an internal random process to produce uncalibrated probabilities that yield
random outputs, or (3) have a systematic process
for producing outputs that appear random enough.
(Previous work would suggest that humans are limited in this regard and will likely not be random
(and therefore not calibrated).) This leaves us with
a one-sided problem. If the humans/models were
proficient at producing random outcomes we would
have to adjudicate between the above possibilities.
In a single-round game, the Nash Equilibrium
is to select a coin face randomly. We set there to
be 100 rounds of play. To focus on calibration, we
frame the tested model as the “misleader.” The
misleader is prompted to submit answers, and the
“guesser” is set to predict the misleader’s answers.
The misleader submits m1 , m2 , . . . , m100 answers,
and the guesser bases each of its gi answers incrementally based upon previous misleader’s answers,
{mj | 0 < j < i}. We use a n-gram9 based strategy

Both best-performing proprietary models and
human behavior are not random. Models are
prompted with the game rules and we explicitly
instruct the models (and humans) to be random.
Not doing so reduces model performance to near 0.
PWR for models and humans are similar, WW for
models is higher, but still low.
Table 8 reports the proportion of samples (where
each sample is 100 coin flips) the result could not
be considered non-random (p = 0.05): Higher
WW values suggest the model is more random.
More model- than human-generated samples were
considered random: 19 − 43% vs. 7%.

Models We focus on gpt-* models sampling
temperature τ = 1. Human behavior is drawn
from a sample of 44 games of 100 rounds from 10
different volunteers with technical backgrounds up
to 10 different games each.
Figure 24 reports our the implementation for the
n-gram model. We find that most n from 1 to 5
do similarly well. In the paper we report a 4-gram
model.
Additional Metrics Whereas previous metrics
rely on model probabilities, this experiment assumes access only to outputs, meaning we cannot
use the metrics used in previous sections.
Player Win Rate (PWR) is the rate the misleader wins, averaging over 100 games each for
up to 100 rounds. The higher this rate, the more
random the outputs of the misleader, and thus the
more calibrated it is at an outcome level.
Randomness Testing (WW). Wald–Wolfowitz
(Wald and Wolfowitz, 1940) tests if the elements
of a sequence are mutually independent. Using
this test at a significance level of 0.05, we report
the proportion of samples that cannot statistically
be rejected as non-random, labeling this value as
WW. For reference, as shown in Table 8 when we
sampled random sequences using python, 98% of
the sequences could not be rejected; only 7% of
human-generated samples could not be rejected.
